title: Cavity-waveguide coupling in phononic crystals
authors: Jakub Rosińński, Benjamin Mayer, Hubert J. Krenner, Paweł Machnikowski
abstract: Phononic crystal platforms provide a promising route toward scalable on-chip quantum networks, where mechanical excitations mediate interactions between solid-state qubits. A key building block of such architectures is the cavity-waveguide system, in which localized mechanical modes couple to propagating phononic modes. However, a quantitative understanding of the mechanisms governing this coupling remains incomplete. In this work, we investigate the interaction between localized modes of snowflake-type phononic crystal cavities and a phononic crystal waveguide using finite-element simulations and experimental measurements. We show that the coupling strength is primarily governed by the spatial overlap between the displacement fields of the corresponding isolated cavity and waveguide modes. After accounting for the effective-mass dependence of the normalized cavity displacement amplitude, we establish a strong correlation between the spatial overlap and the interaction strength across a wide range of mode combinations. Deviations from this leading-order behavior are associated with Bloch-phase effects, variations in waveguide group velocity, and intrinsic hybridization of waveguide modes. Furthermore, we provide experimental evidence for cavity-waveguide coupling in a GaAs phononic crystal membrane by observing a clear resonance in the spectral broadening of the photoluminescence emission from an embedded quantum dot, which serves as a local probe of the mechanical field. The observed resonance at approximately 398 MHz is in good agreement with the corresponding cavity resonance near 395 MHz predicted by finite-element simulations. Our results identify spatial mode overlap as a leading-order design parameter for cavity-waveguide coupling and provide practical guidelines for controlling interactions between localized and propagating modes in phononic crystal structures.
summary: This paper investigates the fundamental physics governing mechanical coupling between localized cavities and propagating waveguides in phononic crystals. Using both finite-element simulations and experimental measurements on GaAs, the authors establish that the coupling strength is predominantly determined by the spatial overlap of the involved vibrational modes. This work provides critical design guidelines for realizing solid-state quantum networks based on phononic interactions.
main_problem: The core problem is understanding and controlling the coupling strength between localized mechanical modes (cavities) and propagating phononic modes (waveguides) within phononic crystals for use in scalable on-chip quantum networks.
main_result: The coupling strength is found to be primarily governed by the spatial overlap between the displacement fields of the isolated cavity and waveguide modes. Experimentally, a clear resonance was observed in the photoluminescence broadening matching simulation predictions.
method: The study employs a combination of finite-element simulations (FEM) to model coupling strength via avoided crossings and experimental measurements using embedded quantum dots (QDs) as local mechanical field probes.
model_or_system: The system involves phononic crystals realized in GaAs, featuring snowflake-type cavities coupled to a waveguide. The interaction mediates coupling between solid-state qubits (like QDs) via mechanical excitations (phonons).
key_observables: Coupling strength (quantified by frequency splitting $\Delta f$), spatial overlap integral ($\eta$), and spectral broadening of photoluminescence emission.
important_parameters: Lattice constant ($a$), cavity radius ($r$), waveguide group velocity ($v_g$), and the spatial overlap integral $\eta$.
main_assumptions: The initial analysis focuses on the leading-order behavior governed by spatial mode overlap, with deviations attributed to Bloch-phase effects and hybridization.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the geometry of the coupled system, show calculated dispersion relations revealing avoided crossings, and present experimental false-color plots showing QD emission modulation mapping out the phononic band gap and cavity resonances.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework by simulating the coupling using FEM, showing the dependence on spatial overlap. It then presents experimental evidence by measuring QD photoluminescence resonance in a fabricated GaAs membrane, confirming the theoretical predictions.
why_interesting: This work provides concrete, quantitative design rules—namely, maximizing spatial mode overlap—for engineering solid-state quantum interconnects using phononics, which is crucial for building scalable quantum networks.
